score_lt.w: A 0–10 summary of the business and its price for a 1–3 year holding: growth, profitability, balance sheet, valuation, quality, dividend, volatility and share count.
score_lt.hi: Higher = a stronger business at a more sensible price.
score_lt.lo: Lower = weaker fundamentals or a price that already asks a lot.
score_lt.lv: 7.5+ strong, 6.2–7.5 favourable, 4.5–6.2 mixed, below 4.5 weak. A screen, not a buy or sell signal.

score_t.w: A 0–10 view of whether conditions favour starting a position in the next 2–12 weeks: trend, momentum, stretch, volatility, a little valuation, and 10% market fear.
score_t.hi: Higher = the price trend and setup support an entry now.
score_t.lo: Lower = the trend is against you or the price is stretched.
score_t.lv: 7.5+ favourable, 6.2–7.5 mostly favourable, 4.5–6.2 neutral, below 4.5 unfavourable.

score_tp.w: The entry-timing score adjusted by the latest company guidance, earnings surprises, analyst estimate changes and dated news.
score_tp.hi: Higher = recent news and guidance strengthen the entry case.
score_tp.lo: Lower = news and guidance argue against the price trend.
score_tp.lv: When it differs from entry timing by more than about 1 point, the news is the reason.

grp_growth.w: How fast sales, earnings and free cash flow have grown over 3–5 years.
grp_growth.hi: Faster growth = a bigger business tomorrow, if it lasts.
grp_growth.lo: Slow or negative growth = the business is standing still or shrinking.

grp_profit.w: How much profit the business makes from its sales and its capital.
grp_profit.hi: Higher margins and returns usually mean pricing power and a durable edge.
grp_profit.lo: Low profitability leaves little room for mistakes or downturns.

grp_health.w: Debt and liquidity: can the company pay what it owes?
grp_health.hi: A strong balance sheet survives recessions and can buy back shares cheaply.
grp_health.lo: Heavy debt makes the shares fragile when profits fall.
grp_health.lv: For banks and insurers these ratios do not apply (n/a).

grp_value.w: What you pay for the profits and cash flows: earnings yield, EV/EBITDA, free-cash-flow yield and cash returned to shareholders.
grp_value.hi: A higher valuation score = cheaper shares for what the business earns.
grp_value.lo: A low score = an expensive price; when below 4/10 its weight rises so a great business at an extreme price cannot score top marks.

grp_quality.w: Signals of earnings quality: Piotroski F-score, manipulation risk (Beneish), cash backing of profits, margin stability, and how fast the balance sheet expands.
grp_quality.hi: Higher = profits are real, stable and backed by cash.
grp_quality.lo: Lower = profits may be fragile or flattered by accounting.

grp_div.w: Dividend yield, how much of profit is paid out, and dividend growth.
grp_div.hi: Higher = a growing, well-covered income stream.
grp_div.lo: Lower = little dividend, or one at risk of a cut.

grp_tech.w: Price behaviour. In the long-term score only volatility counts now (calmer stocks have tended to do as well with less risk); trend, momentum and stretch count in entry timing.
grp_tech.hi: Higher = calmer price (long-term) or a stronger trend (timing).
grp_tech.lo: Lower = wild swings or a downtrend.

grp_mkt.w: In the long-term score: the change in share count (buybacks vs dilution). Earnings surprises and estimate changes count once, in the third score.
grp_mkt.hi: Higher = the company buys back shares.
grp_mkt.lo: Lower = the company issues shares and dilutes owners.

revCagr5.w: Average yearly growth of sales over five years.
revCagr5.hi: Higher = a fast-growing business (15%+ is fast for a large company).
revCagr5.lo: Low or negative = sales are flat or shrinking.
revCagr5.lv: Above ~4% beats the economy's long-run growth.

revCagr3.w: Average yearly growth of sales over three years: a more recent view.
revCagr3.lo: Lower = growth is slowing or negative.

epsCagr5.w: Average yearly growth of earnings per share over five years.
epsCagr5.hi: Higher = profit per share is compounding.
epsCagr5.lo: Lower = profit per share is flat or falling.
epsCagr5.lv: Buybacks raise EPS growth even when total profit grows slowly.

fcfCagr5.w: Average yearly growth of the cash left after investment.
fcfCagr5.hi: Higher = more cash each year to pay dividends, buy back shares or invest.

revYoY.w: Sales growth in the latest year only. Context, not scored.
revYoY.hi: A jump can mean acceleration, or a one-off.
revYoY.lo: A drop can signal a slowdown; one year says little alone.

epsYoY.w: Earnings-per-share change in the latest year. Context, not scored.
epsYoY.lo: Lower = a weak year; one-off items often distort it.

gross.w: Share of each sale left after the direct cost of making the product.
gross.lo: Lower = a commodity-like business where price wars hurt.

op.w: Profit from the core business as a share of sales, before interest and tax.
op.hi: Higher = an efficient, profitable business (20%+ is excellent).
op.lo: Lower = thin profits that a downturn can wipe out.

net.w: Final profit as a share of sales. Context only: it repeats what gross and operating margins show.
net.hi: Higher = more of each sale kept as profit.
net.lo: Lower = little left after costs, interest and tax.

fcfM.w: Cash generated per unit of sales after paying for investment.
fcfM.hi: Higher = the business throws off cash (15%+ is strong).
fcfM.lo: Lower or negative = growth or operations consume cash.

roe.w: Net profit divided by shareholders' equity. Context only: debt and buybacks inflate it.
roe.hi: Higher = owners' money earns a lot.
roe.lo: Lower = weak returns on owners' money.

roe5.w: Return on equity averaged over five years. Context only.

roic.w: After-tax operating profit divided by all the capital invested (debt + equity − cash).
roic.hi: Higher = each euro invested earns a lot (15%+ is excellent).
roic.lo: Below the cost of capital (~8–10%) = growth destroys value.

gpa.w: Gross profit divided by total assets: how productive the asset base is.
gpa.hi: Higher = a more profitable business; a well-documented quality signal (Novy-Marx 2013).

ndEbitda.w: Years of operating profit needed to repay debt minus cash.
ndEbitda.hi: Higher = more leverage (above 3× is high, above 5× risky).
ndEbitda.lo: Below 0 = more cash than debt (net cash).

intCov.w: Operating profit divided by interest paid.
intCov.hi: Higher = interest is easy to pay (above 8× is comfortable).
intCov.lo: Below 2× = interest eats most of the profit.

de.w: Total debt divided by shareholders' equity.
de.hi: Higher = more borrowed money (above 150% is high).

current.w: Short-term assets divided by bills due within a year.
current.hi: Higher = bills are well covered; above 2 earns no extra credit.
current.lo: Below 1 = short-term debts exceed short-term assets.

quick.w: Like the current ratio but without inventory. Context only.
quick.hi: Higher = bills covered without selling stock.

pe.w: Share price divided by the last 12 months of earnings per share: how many years of current profit you pay.
pe.hi: Higher = more expensive (above 30 is pricey unless growth is fast).
pe.lo: Lower = cheaper (below 12 can be a bargain or a warning).
pe.lv: The S&P 500 long-run average is about 16–17.

peFwd.w: Price divided by next year's expected earnings.
peFwd.lo: Lower = cheap on forecasts, if the forecasts hold.

peg.w: P/E divided by the earnings growth rate. Context only.
peg.lo: Below 1 = cheap for the growth, if the growth is real.

ps.w: Market value divided by yearly sales.
ps.hi: Higher = expensive per euro of sales.
ps.lo: Lower = cheap per euro of sales; useful for loss-making firms.
ps.lv: Compare within the industry: margins differ a lot.

pfcf.w: Market value divided by free cash flow. Context only: the exact inverse of the FCF yield, which is scored.

evEbitda.w: Price of the whole business (shares + net debt) divided by operating profit before depreciation.

fcfY.w: Free cash flow divided by market value: the cash return for the price.
fcfY.lo: Lower = expensive (below 2% means you pay for future growth).

shY.w: (Dividends + buybacks − new shares issued) divided by market value: cash returned to owners each year.
shY.hi: Higher = generous cash returns (5%+ is high).
shY.lo: Lower or negative = little returned, or owners diluted.

impG.w: Reverse DCF: the yearly free-cash-flow growth, forever, that today's price assumes. Context only.
impG.hi: Above ~4% = the price assumes growth faster than the economy for ever.
impG.lo: Near 0–2% = modest expectations; the price needs little growth.

pb.w: Price divided by book value (assets minus debts). Scored only for banks and insurers.
pb.hi: Higher = paying more for each euro of net assets.
pb.lo: Below 1 = trading under book value: cheap, or doubts about asset quality.

piotroski.w: Nine yes/no tests on profitability, debt and efficiency trends.

beneish.w: A statistical test for earnings manipulation risk.

altman.lv: Not meaningful for banks and insurers.

conv.w: Whether reported profit turns into cash.
conv.lo: Low = profits may be flattered by accounting or tied up in working capital.

gmStab.w: How much the gross margin moved over five years (percentage points).
gmStab.hi: Higher = unstable margins, weaker pricing power.
gmStab.lo: Lower = steady margins, a durable business.

assetG.w: How fast total assets grew last year.
assetG.hi: Fast expansion (above ~20%) has tended to be followed by lower returns (big acquisitions, over-investment).
assetG.lo: Modest growth is a quiet positive.

capexAb.w: Capital spending vs the company's own usual level, relative to sales.
capexAb.hi: A surge = heavy investment; has tended to precede weaker returns, worse if debt-funded.
capexAb.lo: Normal or lower = no over-investment signal.

spread.w: Return on capital minus the cost of that capital. Context only.
spread.hi: Positive = each euro invested creates value.

divY.w: Yearly dividend per share divided by the price.
divY.hi: Higher = more income; above ~9% often signals a coming cut.

payout.w: Share of earnings paid as dividends.
payout.hi: Above ~75% = little room; a bad year can force a cut.
payout.lo: Below 50% = well covered with room to grow.

divCagr.w: Average yearly growth of the dividend.
divCagr.lo: Low or negative = stagnant or cut dividends.

streak.w: Consecutive years of dividend increases. Context only.

rsi.w: Speed of recent price moves on a 0–100 scale.
rsi.hi: Above 70 = overbought: strong, but often pauses.
rsi.lo: Below 30 = oversold: weak, but often bounces.

macd.w: Gap between short- and long-term price averages. Context only.

adx.w: Strength of the trend, not its direction. Context only.

boll.w: Where the price sits in its 20-day volatility band.
boll.hi: Above 1 = above the upper band, stretched.
boll.lo: Below 0 = below the lower band, washed out.

s200.w: How far the price is above or below its average of the last 200 trading days: the long-term trend.
s200.lv: Many investors treat the 200-day line as the bull/bear dividing line.

stack.w: Two checks: price above its 200-day average, and 50-day average above the 200-day.
stack.lv: 50-day crossing above the 200-day = 'golden cross'; below = 'death cross'.

mom.w: Return over the last 12 months, skipping the latest month, divided by volatility.
mom.hi: Higher = strong medium-term momentum, which has tended to persist for months.
mom.lo: Lower = laggard; weak stocks tend to stay weak for a while.

vol.w: How much the price swings, on a yearly basis.
vol.hi: Higher = bumpier ride (40%+ is very volatile).
vol.lo: Lower = calmer (below 20%); calmer stocks have done about as well with less risk.

hi52.w: How far the price is below its highest price of the past year.
hi52.hi: Close to 0% = near the high; such stocks have tended to keep outperforming.

rev1m.w: Last month's return; counts in timing only.
rev1m.hi: A big gain tends to be partly given back.
rev1m.lo: A big loss tends to partly rebound.

ext50.w: How many average daily ranges the price sits above its 50-day average.
ext50.hi: Above +4 = stretched; entries from here tend to give back.

rvol.w: Recent trading volume vs the months before. Context only.

rs.hi: Positive = the stock leads the market.

upside.w: Analysts' average target vs the current price. Context only: targets lag prices.
upside.hi: Higher = analysts see room to rise.
upside.lo: Negative = the price is above targets.

beta.w: How much the stock moves when the market moves. Context only.
beta.hi: Above 1 = swings more than the market.
beta.lv: Used to scale the market-fear effect per stock.

dilut.w: Yearly change in the number of shares.
dilut.lo: Negative = buybacks: each share owns more of the business.

surprise.w: Reported earnings vs analysts' forecasts, last two quarters. Scored once, in the third score.
surprise.hi: A beat tends to be followed by weeks of upward drift.
surprise.lo: A miss tends to be followed by drift down.

revision.w: Change in analysts' next-year earnings forecast over three months. Scored once, in the third score.

ter.w: The yearly fee taken from the fund.
ter.hi: Higher = more of your return goes to the issuer.
ter.lo: Lower = cheaper (0.05–0.2% for large index funds).

td.w: Fund return minus index return per year: the real cost of holding.
td.hi: Close to 0 or positive = efficient fund.
td.lo: More negative = the fund lags its index.

te.w: How much the gap to the index wobbles.

bas.w: Cost of buying and selling once on the exchange.
bas.lo: Lower = cheap to trade (below 0.1% is good).

aum.hi: Larger = cheaper to run and less likely to close.

adv.w: How much trades each day on the exchange.

prem.w: Gap between the fund's price and the value of what it holds.
prem.hi: Large gaps = you may overpay or sell too cheap.

nhold.w: How many securities the fund owns.

top10.w: Share of the fund in its 10 largest holdings.
top10.hi: Higher = concentrated in a few names.

repl.w: Physical (owns the shares) or synthetic (uses a swap).
repl.lo: Synthetic = adds counterparty risk but can track better.

ipe.w: Price / earnings of the whole index.

ifpe.w: Price / next-year expected earnings of the index.

pedev.w: How many standard deviations the index P/E sits from its 10-year average.

idy.w: Dividends of the holdings divided by price.
idy.hi: Higher = more income, often a cheaper market.

eyg.w: Index earnings yield minus the 10-year government yield: a rough equity risk premium.
eyg.hi: Higher = stocks pay more than bonds.
eyg.lo: Low or negative = stocks expensive vs bonds.

mdd.w: Worst peak-to-trough fall in three years.
mdd.hi: A deeper fall = more pain endured.

sharpe.w: Return above cash divided by volatility.
sharpe.hi: Above 1 = good reward for the risk.

cagr3.w: Past yearly return over three years. Context only.
cagr3.lo: Lower = weak recent past; past returns don't predict much.

cyc.w: Where the coin stands in its cycle: accumulation (price below holders' average cost), bull (above its 200-day average), bear (below it) or distribution (holders on very large profits).
cyc.hi: Accumulation has given the best one-year returns historically.
cyc.lo: Bear and distribution phases have given the worst.

mvrv.w: Market value divided by realised value: today's price divided by the average price at which all coins last moved. A cost-basis ratio, not an intrinsic value.
mvrv.hi: Above 3–3.5 = holders on huge profits; past cycle tops (2013, 2017, 2021) came near there, though peaks have been lower each cycle.
mvrv.lo: Below 1 = the average holder is at a loss; past bear-market bottoms (2015, 2018, 2022) came there.
mvrv.lv: BTC peaks: about 5.9 (2013), 4.7 (2017), 4.0 (2021), 2.7 (2025): don't wait for old top levels.

mvrvP.w: Rank of today's MVRV among the last four years. Context only.

adg.w: Change in the number of addresses using the network. Context only.
adg.lo: Falling = less use; not a reliable price predictor.

fund.w: What leveraged long traders pay short traders on perpetual futures, shown per year.
fund.hi: Above ~30%/yr = crowded leveraged longs: risk of a long squeeze.
fund.lo: Negative = shorts pay longs: pessimism; often near short-term lows.

cfng.w: A 0–100 sentiment index for crypto. Context only.
cfng.lo: Below 25 = fear; gave no reliable contrarian edge in 2018–2026.

w_earn.w: The company's next results date. A report inside the 2–12 week window can move the price more than any indicator.
w_earn.hi: Inside the window = event risk, either way.
w_earn.lo: After the window = no report risk for the timing view.

w_regime.w: Whether the broad market (S&P 500 or a regional index) is above its 200-day average and whether its 50-day is above the 200-day.
w_regime.hi: Above both = a supportive market: new positions work more often.
w_regime.lo: Below = a hostile market: breakouts fail more often.

w_fear.w: A 0–10 score from the fear cycle (VIX phase) and the variance risk premium. It counts for 10% of entry timing for stocks and ETFs (scaled by beta).
w_fear.lo: 4.5 or less = unsupportive (just after fear, or no premium).

fear_phase.w: Where the market is in a stress episode: calm, early fear, peak stress, fading fear (confirmed or not), after fear.
fear_phase.hi: 'Fading fear (confirmed)' has historically been the best entry phase.
fear_phase.lo: 'Early fear' and 'after fear' have been the weakest.
fear_phase.lv: Phases from VIX vs its 1-year range and vs VIX3M, with checks on credit, new lows and bear markets.

vix.w: The market's expected volatility of the S&P 500 over the next 30 days, from option prices: the 'fear gauge'.
vix.hi: Above 30 = high fear; closes above 40 came near the 2008–09, 2010, 2011, 2020 and 2025 lows (but in late 2008 prices still fell much further).
vix.lo: Below 13–15 = calm, sometimes complacent; sharp corrections have started from very low VIX (January 2018, July 2024).

vix3m.w: 30-day expected volatility divided by 3-month expected volatility (term structure).
vix3m.hi: Above 1 = inverted: near-term panic, seen in only a small share of days.

vrp.w: How much options price in beyond the volatility actually expected (VIX² minus a forecast of realised variance).
vrp.hi: A high premium has preceded better stock returns (Bollerslev, Tauchen & Zhou 2009).
vrp.lo: A low or negative premium = realised swings already exceed what options price: less reward for risk.

fade_checks.w: Three tests that confirm fear is really fading: credit has stopped widening, no new 20-day low in the S&P 500 in 5 days, and no bear state.
fade_checks.hi: All three pass = fading fear confirmed.
fade_checks.lo: Any fails = unconfirmed: in 2008 and 2022 such pauses came before new lows.

fear_effect.w: How the market-fear score changes this asset's entry-timing score after scaling by its beta.
fear_effect.lo: Below 4.5 = pulls timing down a little.
fear_effect.lv: Maximum effect is small: about ±0.35 point on the 0–10 timing score.

fear_compare.w: The live reading next to the last official close and the reading a week ago, so you can see the direction.

w_credit.w: What bond lenders are saying: credit spreads, bond funds vs Treasuries, the 10-year yield and a stocks-vs-credit check. Context only.
w_credit.hi: Easing = lenders calm: consistent with steady stocks.
w_credit.lo: Widening = lenders worried: has tended to come before or with weaker stocks.

hy.w: Extra yield that risky ('junk') companies pay over Treasuries (ICE BofA index, FRED).
hy.hi: Above 6% = stress, above 8% = crisis (2001–02 about 10–11%, 2008 peak about 21.8%, 2020 peak about 10.9%).
hy.lo: Below 3% = very tight: late-cycle complacency (2007, 2021, late 2024).
hy.lv: Long-run average about 5%. Equity bottoms came within about three months of spread peaks in 2009, 2016, 2020 and 2022.

ig.w: Extra yield that solid, highly rated companies pay over Treasuries.

ccc.w: Extra yield on the riskiest junk bonds (rated CCC and below). They show stress first.
ccc.hi: Above 12% = serious stress; above 15–20% = crisis (2020 about 20%, 2008 above 40%).
ccc.lo: Below 7% = easy money for weak borrowers (2021, 2024).
ccc.lv: Watch the change: CCC widening faster than all high yield = trouble concentrated in weak firms.

fund_adj.w: Corporate bond funds (HYG, LQD) vs a Treasury fund (IEF), with the interest-rate effect removed.
fund_adj.hi: Positive = corporate bonds beat Treasuries: lenders calm.
fund_adj.lo: Negative = corporate bonds lag: lenders worried.

ust10.w: The interest rate on 10-year US government bonds.
ust10.hi: Rising fast (+0.25 pt in a month) = pressure on stock valuations, especially growth stocks.
ust10.lo: Falling = support for valuations; falling while stocks fall = flight to safety.

stk_cr.w: Checks whether stocks and credit tell the same story.
stk_cr.hi: Stocks up while credit weakens = the rally is not confirmed by bonds.
stk_cr.lo: Stocks down while credit holds = the selling is not confirmed.

live_cr.w: Today's move in bond funds vs Treasuries, from live quotes, compared with the last close.

zone.w: A plain reading of where today's fear and credit levels sit compared with past bottoms, bull runs and bear markets. Context only.
zone.hi: Green = conditions that came near past bottoms or in bull runs.
zone.lo: Red = conditions that came before or during declines.
zone.lv: Based on history (1996–2026); markets can go further than ever before. Not a forecast.

w_dir.w: Whether long (buy) or short (sell) setups are favoured by the trend and timing.
w_dir.hi: 'Long setups favoured' = trend and timing line up for buyers.

w_tt.w: Mark Minervini's 8 checks for a 'stage 2' uptrend (moving averages stacked, price near highs, strong relative strength).
w_tt.hi: 5/5 blocks = meets his template: a setup filter, not a buy signal.
w_tt.lo: Few blocks = not in a stage-2 uptrend.

tt_stop.w: A stop level at 2× the average daily range, and his sizing rule (risk at most 1.25% of the portfolio per trade).
tt_stop.hi: A wide stop (above 10%) = too volatile for his rules.
tt_stop.lo: A tight stop = smaller loss if wrong.

tt_ctx.w: Extra entry points he looks at: RS line at a new high, not stretched, no lottery-like spike, volume support, liquidity.

w_exp.w: What the price already assumes (reverse DCF for stocks; valuation vs history for ETFs; price vs holders' average cost for crypto).
w_exp.hi: High expectations = little room for disappointment.
w_exp.lo: Modest expectations = the price needs little growth.

w_etfck.w: Structural checks: leverage or inverse funds, size, price vs NAV, concentration.
w_etfck.hi: Warnings = the fund has a structural issue.

w_file.w: Whether the last reports were filed on time with the regulator, and any warning signs (late filing, restatement, auditor change).
w_file.hi: Warning = a late report or a hard warning sign.

p_regime.w: Context for the whole market: fear, credit, interest rates and inflation. It never changes any score.
p_regime.hi: Supportive readings = a friendlier backdrop for buying.
p_regime.lo: Hostile readings = a tougher backdrop; stocks fall together in bad markets.

us2y.w: Interest rate on 2-year US government bonds. It moves with where markets expect the Fed's rates to go.
us2y.hi: Rising quickly = markets expect higher Fed rates (hawkish): a headwind for stocks.
us2y.lo: Falling = markets expect cuts; if stocks also fall, it can mean recession fears.

real10.w: The 10-year Treasury yield after inflation (TIPS). It is the 'true' cost of money over time.
real10.hi: Above 2% = restrictive; weighs most on expensive growth stocks.
real10.lo: Below 0.5% = easy money; supports high valuations.

curve.hi: Positive and steepening = normal; steepening after an inversion has often come close to recessions.
curve.lo: Negative (inverted) = historically a recession warning (2000, 2006–07, 2019, 2022–24), with long and variable lags.

cpi.hi: Higher than expected = higher rates for longer: a headwind.
cpi.lv: The Fed targets 2% on PCE; monthly 0.2% ≈ 2.4%/yr.

ccpi.w: Consumer inflation without food and energy: the underlying trend.

pce.hi: Higher = pressure to keep rates high.

cpce.w: PCE without food and energy: the number the Fed watches most.
cpce.hi: Above 3% = well above target; 3-month pace above the yearly pace = accelerating.

ppi.w: Prices companies receive for their goods and services (BLS final demand).
ppi.hi: Rising fast = cost pressure that can reach consumer prices and squeeze margins.

inf_trend.w: The last three months annualised compared with the last 12 months.

p_btc.w: Where Bitcoin stands in its cycle, from free data: MVRV (price vs holders' average cost), the 200-day trend, momentum, drawdown and funding. Context only, never scored.
p_btc.hi: Green states = valuation zone, early setup or confirmed recovery.
p_btc.lo: Red states = euphoria warning or defensive (downtrend).
p_btc.lv: Only price trend and MVRV have published evidence; 3–4 cycles are too few to trust any exact level.

btc_state.w: One label among: valuation zone, stress, capitulation, early high-risk setup, confirmed recovery, expansion, euphoria warning, defensive.
btc_state.hi: Confirmed recovery = price back above its 200-day trend with positive momentum after stress.
btc_state.lo: Defensive = below the 200-day with negative momentum: past bear markets lived here.
btc_state.lv: Labels describe, they do not predict.

btc_val.w: MVRV below 1 or in the bottom 10% of its history: holders at a loss on average.
btc_val.hi: Historically the best one-year entry area, but it can last months and prices can fall further.
btc_val.lo: Out of the zone = no deep-value signal.

rp.w: Average price at which all coins last moved on-chain: the market's average cost.
rp.hi: Price far above it = holders on big profits.
rp.lo: Price below it = average holder underwater; past bottoms (2015, 2018, 2022) dipped below it.

ma200.w: The average price of the last 200 days: the long-term trend line.
ma200.lv: Crossing back above after a bear market has marked confirmed recoveries (2019, 2023).

mom90.w: The 90-day return divided by its volatility.
mom90.hi: Above 0 = momentum up; crypto momentum has tended to persist (Liu & Tsyvinski 2021).

ddath.w: How far the price is below its record high.
ddath.lo: Bitcoin bear markets fell about 75–85% (2014, 2018, 2022); a fall of 40%+ marks stress.

vol30.w: How violently the price swings, last 30 days, yearly basis.
vol30.hi: A spike during a fall = forced selling, often near capitulation.
vol30.lo: Low = quiet market; quiet periods often precede big moves.

btc_ffng.w: Leverage (perpetual funding) and the crypto Fear & Greed index.
btc_ffng.lo: Negative funding and extreme fear = pessimism, sometimes near short-term lows.
